guidance: Pick the layout that was active while the text was mistyped, then the layout you meant to type on. Letters, digits and punctuation are matched by physical key, so names, code and prose come back intact; a character the first layout has no key for stays exactly as it is and is listed under the result. Swap flips the direction together with the text.
method: A keyboard sends a key code, and the operating system's layout decides which character that code becomes. Switching layouts therefore changes text by position, not by letter: with Dvorak active the key printed H produces d and the key printed E produces a full stop, so hello arrives as d.nnr. The page holds the ANSI US QWERTY, Dvorak and Colemak tables for the 47 alphanumeric keys (grave, twelve number-row keys, twelve top-row keys, the backslash key, eleven home-row keys and ten bottom-row keys) at both the unshifted and the shifted level, 94 characters per layout. The character typed is looked up in the first layout's reverse table to recover its key and shift level, and the same key and level are read out of the second layout's table. This is an exact, lossless remap for the 94 characters of each layout and is its own inverse: converting a text from Dvorak to QWERTY and back returns it unchanged, which the tests check for every ordered pair of layouts over printable ASCII. Spaces, tabs and line breaks pass through untouched and are not counted. A character that has no key in the first layout, such as an accent, a typographic dash or an emoji, is emitted unchanged, counted separately and listed, so nothing is silently dropped; surrogate pairs are stepped as whole code points. Repeating the conversion in the other direction reproduces the original whenever all characters were typable. Only the unshifted and shifted levels are modelled, so AltGr and dead-key characters are outside its scope, and the international AZERTY and QWERTZ layouts are not included.
